title: The Work Beneath the Work
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. recirculates a 2017 post arguing that teacher burnout at this time of year comes less from the visible workload than from a hidden work beneath it. The visible work, which includes lesson plans, behavior management and 153 students across six periods, can be managed with constraint-based habits like fixed-schedule productivity and saying no more often. The work beneath the work is the drive to use the job to prove ourselves, to matter, to show that teaching is hard, and to be a respected, irreplaceable hero. He confesses that early in his career this drive, modeled on Freedom Writers and The Ron Clark Story, tied his identity to his job. He calls this ceaseless striving soul-twisting slavery because it is entirely about the teacher, while real teaching is other-centered and aims at creating something new in someone else. Teachers who last, he says, keep returning to what the real work is, and longevity is the true mark of greatness.
points: Burnout often comes from a hidden motive layered over the job: proving ourselves, mattering, demonstrating that teaching is hard, or being the irreplaceable hero.
The visible demands of teaching are survivable with constraints such as fixed-schedule productivity and saying no more often.
Stuart names his own early-career drive to be the hero of all his students and warns it tied his identity to his job.
Real teaching is other-centered, making the teacher a tool for passing knowledge, skills and wisdom to the next generation.
Longevity, achieved by repeatedly returning to the real work, is the mark of teaching greatness.
quotes: One of the reasons we tend towards burnout this time of year is that there's a work beneath our work.
But there's a work beneath our work that can make these real-world teaching demands truly disastrous.
And frankly, all of that work — the work beneath the work — is soul-twisting slavery. All of it is 100% about me, just like your work beneath the work is ultimately just about you.
Want to burn yourself out? Submit yourself to the ceaseless striving that such work beneath the work tyrannically calls us to.
Teaching — the real work — is wholly other-centered, totally focused on creating something new in someone else.
Teaching's real work turns the teacher into a tool for one of humanity's oldest magics — the passing on of knowledge, skills, and wisdom from one generation to the next.
The teachers who flourish for the duration — who reach the true mark of teaching greatness, which is longevity — continually bring themselves back to what the real work is.
